lesson.title: Present Tense Drill
lesson.subtitle: werken, maken, leren, lezen, schrijven, spreken

hook.title: Six Verbs, One Machine
hook.content: Read the infinitive, find the stem, choose the ending. Werken, maken, leren, lezen, schrijven, spreken: the same machine runs every one of them.

pattern.title: Stem first, ending second
pattern.content: Werk + t = werkt; lees + t = leest; schrijf + t = schrijft. The spelling of the stem stays; only the final -t or -en is added. Plural forms take the infinitive minus -n? No: they take stem + -en.
pattern.trap_note: Lezen and schrijven change their stem spelling before -t: lees, schrijf. Do not add -t to the infinitive.

exercises.prompt: Match each English meaning with its Dutch twin (Present Tense Drill):
exercises.target_answer: werken, maken, leren, lezen, schrijven, spreken
exercises.meaning: to work, to make, to learn; to teach, to read, to write, to speak
exercises.explanation: These are the anchors of "Present Tense Drill": read each Dutch form through the pattern, not as a new word.
“Ik leer Nederlands.” is the Dutch form; the other readings bend the pattern of “Present Tense Drill”.

cues: The pattern: Stem first, ending second
It means: You read a book.
exercises.explanation: “Jij leest een boek.” puts the thought together the Dutch way — Stem first, ending second.

diagnosis.slip: an English-shaped word order slipped in
diagnosis.cue: Lezen and schrijven change their stem spelling before -t: lees, schrijf. Do not add -t to the infinitive.

exercises.prompt: Which English sentence is built the Dutch way?
exercises.explanation: “Wij schrijven een woord.” is word-for-word “We write a word.”. The odd English is the lesson — never a model to produce. Pattern: Stem first, ending second.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.explanation: “Hij spreekt goed.” reuses only material taught in “Present Tense Drill” — Stem first, ending second.
exercises.affirmation: You heard “Hij spreekt goed.” — a sentence built from the lesson's own Dutch, practising Stem first, ending second.

twist.prompt: One more, no safety net — say: “I make coffee.”
twist.explanation: Maken follows the same stem + ending machine as werken and leren.

summary.outcome: Conjugate six high-frequency verbs in the present tense.
summary.takeaway: Regular verbs are not memorised one by one; they are one stem plus three endings.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on De Brug: Niet & Geen.

werken.etymology_derivation: English work and Dutch werken are the same verb.

maken.etymology_derivation: English make and Dutch maken are the same verb; German shifted k to ch in machen.

leren.etymology_derivation: Dutch leren covers both learning and teaching; English split the meanings.

lezen.etymology_derivation: English read and Dutch lezen are the same verb; the d became z in Dutch.

schrijven.etymology_derivation: From Latin scrībere; English shrive and scribe are the same root in different clothes.

spreken.etymology_derivation: English speak and Dutch spreken are the same verb; German shifted k to ch in sprechen.
